response.assessment: Two proposals executed. Proposal mut-unsafe-param-change-001 produced an XPASS: unsafe fixture returned ACCEPT (tamperedOwnerRecovered=true) where REJECT was expected. This contradicts the hypothesis that changing parameter alters the ACTION encoding in the unsafe hash. The safe fixture returned REJECT where UNKNOWN was expected (INCONCLUSIVE). Proposal mut-gas-above-cap-001 produced a PREDICTED outcome with no observed verdict; the gas finding is an unsigned policy prediction only, not a runtime observation. Key concerns follow.
concerns: XPASS on unsafe fixture: hypothesis held that parameter=99 alters the keccak256(abi.encode(chainid,this,nonce,ACTION)) digest vs parameter=10 original signature, causing recovery failure. Instead tamperedOwnerRecovered=true was observed. This requires scrutiny: either ACTION does not encode the calldata parameter field, or the tool reused the tampered-input signature rather than the original-input signature for recovery against the tampered hash.

The observation reports both authorizedOwnerRecovered=true AND tamperedOwnerRecovered=true for unsafe. If the tool signed with the mutated input (parameter=99) rather than verifying the original (parameter=10) signature against the new hash, the XPASS is a tool artifact, not a contract behavior finding. The evidenceNeeded specified signing for parameter=10 then verifying against parameter=99; it is unclear the executor honored this asymmetry.

canonicalHashChanged=true for unsafe confirms the two hashes differ (0xeebb73... vs 0xc88cab...), so the hash mutation is real. Yet owner recovery succeeded on both. This is only possible if the same private key signed both hashes, implying the tool generated a fresh signature per hash rather than reusing the original. That would invalidate the XPASS as a finding.

Safe fixture REJECT (tamperedOwnerRecovered=false) with canonicalHashChanged=true is consistent with safe-binding to SIG_HASH: the tampered hash differs from the original SIG_HASH-bound value, so recovery fails. This is internally consistent with fact safe-binding but the original expected verdict was UNKNOWN; the result cannot be treated as confirmed without knowing what concrete sig was used.

Proposal mut-gas-above-cap-001 observedVerdict is null; classification is PREDICTED. No runtime execution occurred. The confidence label VERIFIED in the prediction source refers to a cited evidence file not supplied as a fixture here. The gas boundary arithmetic (67201 > 67200) is consistent with facts gas-cap, sender-gas, signature-gas, but the prediction remains unsigned policy only with no live runtime proof.

liveState for all accounts is UNKNOWN (funding, nonce, deployment, stake, runtime). Neither finding can be promoted to a verified vulnerability without runtime confirmation. The XPASS on unsafe is at most a hypothesis-execution-method concern, not a confirmed contract flaw.

The safe REJECT outcome shares the assumption that the same witness (sameWitness=true) was used across both hashes. If the witness is the OWNER key signing the tampered hash directly, both results are artifacts of tool signing behavior, not contract authorization logic.

concerns: XPASS on unsafe fixture: hypothesis held that parameter=99 alters the keccak256(abi.encode(chainid,this,nonce,ACTION)) digest vs parameter=10 original signature, causing recovery failure. Instead tamperedOwnerRecovered=true was observed. This requires scrutiny: either ACTION does not encode the calldata parameter field, or the tool reused the tampered-input signature rather than the original-input signature for recovery against the tampered hash.

The observation reports both authorizedOwnerRecovered=true AND tamperedOwnerRecovered=true for unsafe. If the tool signed with the mutated input (parameter=99) rather than verifying the original (parameter=10) signature against the new hash, the XPASS is a tool artifact, not a contract behavior finding. canonicalHashChanged=true for unsafe confirms the two hashes differ (0xeebb73... vs 0xc88cab...), so the hash mutation is real. Yet owner recovery succeeded on both. This is only possible if the same private key signed both hashes, implying the tool generated a fresh signature per hash rather than reusing the original. That would invalidate the XPASS as a finding.
